newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-U.S Feb PPI seen lower, inflation dormant.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-U.S Feb PPI seen lower, inflation dormant.

text.p: Soft food and energy prices probably depressed overall producer prices for the second month in a row in February, reinforcing the widespread notion that U.S. inflation remains dormant, economists said.

Meanwhile, the core rate, which excludes the more volatile food and energy components, was expected to have risen only slightly as February car and truck prices supposedly held flat due to extensive vehicle rebates, analysts said.

Economists in a Reuters poll were calling for a 0.1 percent decline in the February producer price index (PPI), set for release 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Friday, March 14, following a 0.3 percent fall in January. The core rate was expected, on average, to rise a benign 0.1 percent after a flat reading in January.
The last time the PPI decreased for two consecutive months was in September and October of 1994, economists said.
Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp, said the Federal Reserve and capital markets were likely to view the data as "something that could hurt, but can't help."

A significantly stronger-than-expected reading could prod Fed policymakers to rein in inflation pressures at their next meeting on March 25 by raising short-term rates, and a greater threat of higher rates would weigh heavily on debt markets.

Dana Johnson, head of economic research at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc, said the Fed will not only look at finished producer goods prices, but will also "look with considerable intensity" at prices in the earlier stages of production.
"The Fed, like the market, is anticipating a pretty tame number at the finished goods level given that there hasn't been much of a build-up at the earlier stage of processing," Johnson said.
"But there are little-bit-worse trends beginning to emerge," he added, referring to the two percent January increase in core crude goods.
Research by Dean Witter Reynolds' economics team said input prices are a key indicator to watch since they measure supply and demand imbalances and are a sign of potential inflation pressures.
"The only problem area could be the core crude price indices, which have the potential to be less friendly to the market than in the past," the report said.

Economists were quick to note that inflation is a lagging indicator and that finished goods prices in particular lag developments in the real economy. Also, recent comments by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan suggest the central bank currently is focused more on wage than final product inflation.
Alexy said the scheduled Wednesday afternoon release of the Beige Book, the Fed's economic outlook which is published every six weeeks, will set the tone for the market reaction to the PPI.
"If there is an alarmist tone in the Beige Book, then any kind of commodity inflation would be viewed as a negative," Alexy said.
Analysts expect January's unwinding of last year's run-up in energy prices to have continued in February.

Energy prices jumped almost 17 percent on an annualized basis in the last half of 1996 before falling 0.2 percent in January. A roughly one percent drop is anticipated in February energy prices, reflecting lower gasoline, electricity and heating oil prices, economists said.
Among other components, economists said that apparel, capital equipment and coffee prices may have ticked higher, but this was most likely offset by a drop in computer and meats prices.
